newsitem.title: USA: Clinton faces touchy issues at news conference.
newsitem.headline: Clinton faces touchy issues at news conference.

text.p: President Bill Clinton faced likely questioning on some touchy issues on Tuesday at the first news conference of his second term, including political fundraising and the health of Russian President Boris Yeltsin.

White House officials said Clinton, who took office for another four-year term eight days ago, would open the 2:30 p.m. EST (1930 GMT) session with a proposal to spend $500 million to link U.S. schools to the Internet and otherwise improve education technology.
U.S. presidents usually lead off these encounters by spotlighting some project or achievement. Reporters just as regularly change the subject at the first opportunity.
One likely basis for questioning on Tuesday was what effect Yeltsin's uncertain health may have on U.S.-Russian relations including a planned early summit with Clinton.

An even hotter topic for American audiences was the prospect of congressional inquiries into much-criticised White House campaign fund-raising tactics -- a centre of controversy since it was revealed during Clinton's re-election campaign last year that Democrats had solicited large sums from Asian business interests with a stake in U.S. trade policy.

Congressional Republicans say two of Clinton's second-term Cabinet nominations -- Labour Secretary-designate Alexis Herman and Transportation Secretary-designate Rodney Slater -- could be in for a rough time in required Senate confirmation hearings because of apparent involvement in questionable fund-raising on his behalf.

"Whatever the line (on legitimate fund-raising) is, the White House seems to have pushed it as far as it can," said Joe Karpinski, a spokesman for Sen. James Jeffords, a Vermont Republican who will chair Herman's confirmation hearings.

Documents released by the White House in advance of the hearings showed that top administration officials, including Herman and Slater, helped execute a highly detailed plan to build support for Clinton among various constituent groups, including African, Asian, Jewish and disabled Americans.
The underlying issue in the fund-raising controversy -- including Republican efforts as well -- is whether the efforts crossed the line into plain influence-peddling.

The latest disclosure to raise eyebrows involved a May 1996 White House coffee meeting at which Clinton brought bankers and banking regulators together, with Democratic Party fundraisers sitting in on the discussion.

He maintains that he and his party did nothing wrong. But White House officials said he would "strongly reiterate" his support for campaign finance reform, perhaps in his opening statement at the White House East Room news conference.
The officials said the main thrust of Clinton's opening statement, however, would be spending proposals for education.
They said he would announce that the budget he will send Congress on Feb. 6 will call for increasing the Technology Literacy Challenge Fund to $425 million in the fiscal year starting next Oct. 1.

The fund gives U.S. schools federal money for Internet access and education technology in an effort to meet Clinton's goal of having a computer in every classroom by the year 2000. It currently totals $200 million.
Clinton also plans to seek about $75 million to encourage public-private high-tech educational partnerships, officials said. The current budget earmarks $57 million for this.
Clinton has said he wants $29 billion in overall education spending next year, $2.7 billion more than this year.
